o: Per data center i we have count[i] servers, upgrade cost u = upgrade[i] per upgraded server, sell price s = sell[i] per sold server, and budget m = money[i]. Selling some servers funds upgrading others; maximize the number upgraded, independently per center. Example 1, center 1: selling 1 server gives 8+4 = 12, enough to upgrade the remaining 3 (cost 9) — answer 3. Center 2: sell 1 → 11, upgrade 2 (cost 10) — answer 2. Example 2: with 1 server, selling it leaves nothing to upgrade, and 1 < 2 so answer 0. If we upgrade u servers we sell count−u of them, needing u·u ≤ m + (count−u)·s, i.e. u·(u+s) ≤ m + count·s — solvable in closed form or by binary search.
k: Upgrading u servers implies selling count−u servers, giving the feasibility inequality u·(upgrade+sell) ≤ money + count·sell.
Closed form: u = min(count, (money + count·sell) // (upgrade + sell)); binary search on u works equally well.

a.i: Rewrite the budget constraint as u·(u+s) ≤ m + c·s (selling all non-upgraded servers maximizes available funds, and selling more never hurts). Hence the maximal u is ⌊(m + c·s)/(u+s)⌋, clamped to c. One division per center gives an O(n) solution.
s: For each center compute denom = upgrade + sell and cap = money + count·sell.
Append u to the answer array.
a.t: O(n) — constant work per data center.

a.n: Approach 2: Binary search on the answer
a.i: Feasibility of upgrading u servers is monotone: if u servers can be upgraded, so can u−1 (sell one fewer). Needed sales for target u are sNeeded = max(0, ⌈(u·upgrade − money)/sell⌉), and u is feasible iff u + sNeeded ≤ count. Binary search the largest feasible u in [0, count] per center — O(n log C), slightly slower but a robust template when the feasibility predicate is complicated.
s: Define feasible(u): need = max(0, u·upgrade − money); sells = ceil(need / sell); return u + sells ≤ count.
Binary search u in [0, count] for the largest feasible value.
a.t: O(n log C) with C ≤ 10⁵ — a binary search per center over the upgrade count.

w: Present the closed form as the optimal answer and the binary search as the generalizable fallback — interviewers often probe 'what if selling had diminishing returns?' where monotone-feasibility + binary search still applies. Pitfalls: 64-bit arithmetic (count·sell reaches 10¹⁰), remembering the clamp min(·, count) when money already covers everything, and the subtle point that selling extra servers is always allowed (leftover money is simply unused). Follow-ups: shared budget across centers (greedy by best ratio), or upgrade discounts for bulk purchases (breaking the linear feasibility used here).
